'''

Linux kernel vs user space, file system navigation, permissions (chmod, chown), users and…

Linux permissions enforce discretionary access control boundaries between unprivileged user-space processes and protected kernel resources. Path traversal requires search rights on every parent directory, and process credentials determine mode bit selection before files can be opened.

Why today: Establishes the foundational host security and access control boundaries governing application processes, container runtimes, and local configuration files.

Where it sits: Sits at the base of local host operating system management, establishing directory and credential constraints before supervising background processes.

Problem preview: A deployed order processing daemon crashes on startup with an EACCES permission denied error while reading its configuration file. Investigation reveals that the file was created by an administrative deployer with owner-only read permissions, preventing the unprivileged service user from accessing the configuration.

Processes, file descriptors (stdin/stdout/stderr), pipes, redirection, boot-to-service…

Process supervision governs the execution, I/O streams, and lifecycle transitions of operating system services from initialization to shutdown. Systemd orchestrates unit dependency graphs, tracks process IDs, captures standard streams into system journals, and manages graceful termination via signals.

Why today: Provides the execution runtime and operational observability model underpinning virtual machine daemons, background workers, and containerized microservices.

Where it sits: Operates on top of filesystem permissions to govern active daemon execution, directly producing the service lifecycle timestamps required for exit evidence.

Problem preview: An order fulfillment worker restarted during a deployment generates duplicate customer shipments for in-flight queue messages. A forced SIGKILL termination interrupted the worker after shipping the goods but before committing completion state, causing the message broker to redeliver the unacknowledged event to a replacement instance.

'''

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: Linux separates privileged kernel-mode execution from unprivileged user-mode execution. On x86, Ring 0 hosts the Kernel Space, managing CPU registers, virtual memory translation, page tables, interrupts, and devices visible to that kernel; a guest kernel remains subject to its virtualization boundary. On x86, Ring 3 hosts User Space, where unprivileged applications and system daemons execute within isolated virtual address spaces; other processor architectures use their own privilege mechanisms. User-space programs request protected kernel operations through System Calls (syscalls) such as open(), read(), write(), and fork(), which enter kernel mode through architecture-specific instructions. A privilege transition need not switch the scheduler to a different process; some user-visible library operations can also complete without a syscall.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud architects designing compute infrastructure must understand that container engines (e.g., Docker, containerd) share the host Linux kernel; a container is simply an isolated user-space process group governed by cgroups and namespaces. Unlike hypervisor virtual machines with distinct guest kernels, vulnerabilities in the host kernel system call interface can lead to container escape and privilege escalation across multi-tenant workloads.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to GCP:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to GCP: On a Linux Compute Engine guest, investigate the requesting process and guest kernel before interpreting a configuration read failure as a cloud networking fault. OS Login links Google identities to Linux login access through IAM permissions; that login integration does not let ordinary application code bypass the guest kernel boundary. Architectural application: keep the syscall caller, Linux authorization decision and cloud login identity separate in the worksheet. The diagram is about the guest syscall boundary, not a deployment or proof of a container sandbox.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: Linux structures all stored entities into a single, unified hierarchical tree rooted at /, adhering to the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS). The kernel provides the Virtual File System (VFS) abstraction layer, providing uniform system-call semantics regardless of underlying storage formats (ext4, XFS, tmpfs, NFS, or block-backed persistent disks). When resolving a path like /srv/brightloaf/order-api/config.json, the kernel iteratively looks up each directory component (dentry), verifying search (execute) permission on every parent directory in sequence. Read permission lists directory entries; it is not required to traverse a known pathname.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Path resolution failure is a common root cause of deployment failures: even if a file has world-readable mode 0644, an unprivileged service account cannot open it if any parent directory (e.g. /srv/brightloaf) lacks the execute (traverse) bit for that user or group. Cloud architects design predictable, standard mount points for persistent volumes and ensure container volume mounts do not mask parent directory permissions.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to GCP:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to GCP: For a Linux guest hosted on Compute Engine, distinguish login access from local path authorization. OS Login centralizes login management, but an application still uses its working directory and process credentials to resolve the mounted guest namespace. Architectural application: check the mount, every searchable parent directory and the final file under the service identity. A path in a cloud storage product is not automatically a POSIX guest path; the example establishes no filesystem or FUSE deployment.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: Standard Linux file permissions are stored as 12 Mode Bits in the file inode: 3 special bits (setuid, setgid, sticky) and 9 permission bits divided into three classes: Owner (User), Group, and Other (World). Each class has three permissions: Read (r, 4), Write (w, 2), and Execute (x, 1). Crucially, the execute bit on a directory grants search/traverse rights—the ability to pass through the directory to access children. Without execute permission on a directory, no child files can be accessed regardless of their individual file mode bits.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Granting world-writable (0777) permissions to resolve application startup failures is a catastrophic security anti-pattern that violates enterprise compliance (CIS Benchmarks, PCI-DSS). Architects enforce least-privilege mode bits (e.g. 0750 for directories, 0640 for configuration files containing credentials, and 0600 for private keys) and automate permission linting in CI/CD container image pipelines.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to GCP:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to GCP: OS Login manages IAM-linked access to Linux instances; its benefits section does not specify universal home-directory modes or application configuration ownership. Set deployment mode bits deliberately, then inspect the actual guest inode and parent directories. Architectural application: a successful IAM login is a prerequisite for a host investigation, not proof that an unprivileged daemon can read a credential file. Keep 0640 and 0750 as this example’s design choices rather than provider defaults.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: Every Linux process executes under a set of kernel credentials: a Real User ID (RUID), an Effective User ID (EUID) used for permission checks, a Real Group ID (RGID), an Effective Group ID (EGID), and an array of Supplementary Groups. When a process issues an open() system call, the kernel evaluates credentials in strict priority: (1) If process EUID matches file owner UID, owner bits apply; (2) Else if process EGID or any supplementary GID matches file GID, group bits apply; (3) Otherwise, other bits apply. Evaluation stops at the first matching class—if the user matches the owner class and owner bits deny read, group bits are never checked.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Service accounts running microservices must never execute as UID 0 (root). Architects establish dedicated non-login system accounts (e.g. UID 10001, shell /sbin/nologin) and assign supplementary group memberships to grant access to shared configuration or unix sockets, ensuring isolation between distinct microservice daemons on the same virtual host.

Architectural application: compare the account profile with the running process credentials before attributing a denied read to IAM. The local model uses numeric IDs without provisioning Google identities or changing group membership; this evidence cannot prove an OS Login integration worked.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: Linux file ownership is established by the file's UID and GID, modified via the chown and group-changing operations exposed through chgrp. Changing owner requires appropriate privilege; an unprivileged file owner can change the group to one of that owner’s groups. To perform privileged maintenance, Linux systems employ sudo (superuser do) to temporarily elevate privileges based on rules defined in /etc/sudoers. Sudo delegation allows operators to execute specific commands as root or as service identities without sharing the root password or granting unbounded shell access.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud architects mandate least privilege by restricting sudo permissions to specific immutable administrative binaries and prohibiting interactive root shells (sudo su -). Auditing sudo execution via systemd journals and centralized security SIEMs provides tamper-evident logs for SOC2 and ISO 27001 compliance.

paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to GCP: OS Login documents centralized Linux login management and the ability to configure administrator access. Separate that administrative entry point from the least-privilege identity used by an application service. Architectural application: document who may change config.json ownership, who may read it and which privileged maintenance operations are allowed; do not infer arbitrary application-group access from a successful login. The exercise changes only disposable file modes and installs no sudo policy or production account.

paragraphs.label: Concrete example:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Concrete example: An automated deployment pipeline copies an application configuration file to /srv/brightloaf/order-api/config.json under the administrative deployment user identity deploy-admin:deploy-admin with mode 0600 (read/write only for owner). When the systemd service starts, it drops privileges to execute under the dedicated service user order-api (UID 10001, GID 10001). The service attempts to open config.json for reading. The kernel checks process EUID (10001) against file owner UID (10000); they mismatch. The kernel checks process EGID (10001) against file GID (10000); they mismatch. The kernel evaluates the "other" permission class, which is 0 (no access). The kernel halts the system call and returns EACCES (Permission denied). To remediate without granting world-readable access, the administrator changes group ownership to order-api and sets mode 0640 (owner read/write, group read, other none), restoring access for the service while protecting credentials from other local accounts.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: A Process is an executing instance of a program, encapsulating an isolated virtual memory address space (code, data, heap, stack), a set of file descriptors, and kernel execution state. In Linux, new processes are created via the fork() (or clone()) system call, creating a child process that inherits memory pages with copy-on-write (COW) semantics. The child typically invokes execve() to replace its address space with a new executable. Each process receives a unique integer Process ID (PID) allocated by the kernel, managed under PID 1 (systemd or init), which adopts orphaned processes and reaps terminating zombie processes.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Understanding the process lifecycle is foundational for container and VM architecture. In container environments, PID 1 inside the container namespace must properly forward signals to child processes and reap zombie processes to prevent PID exhaustion. Furthermore, architects size memory limits based on process resident set size (RSS) rather than virtual memory size (VMS) to prevent kernel Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminations.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to GCP:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to GCP: On a systemd-based Linux guest, use the manager and guest process evidence to investigate worker lifecycle; the chosen guest image determines its init system. OS Login provides an IAM-linked administrative access path, not a guarantee that every Compute Engine image uses systemd or every application is PID 1. Architectural application: record the actual manager, MainPID and timestamp before comparing service restarts. The local user-service checkpoint tests supervision without deploying a VM, container or guest agent.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: When a Linux process is launched, its launcher conventionally supplies three standard File Descriptors (FDs): 0 (Standard Input, stdin), 1 (Standard Output, stdout), and 2 (Standard Error, stderr). Through Pipelines (|), the shell connects the stdout of one process to the stdin of another via a unidirectional kernel pipe buffer. Through I/O Redirection (>, >>, 2>&1), stdout and stderr streams can be redirected to disk files, special character devices (like /dev/null), or Unix domain sockets.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud observability relies on standard stream hygiene: Twelve-Factor Application design mandates that microservices write all diagnostic logs directly to stdout and stderr rather than internal rotating log files. This decouples the application from local disk storage and enables cloud container runtimes and logging agents to aggregate, parse, and forward log streams centrally.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: When a Linux virtual machine boots, the kernel mounts the root filesystem and executes PID 1 (systemd). Systemd organizes services, mount points, sockets, and targets into declarative Unit Files. Units declare dependencies using directives like Wants=, Requires=, After=, and Before=, compiling an asynchronous directed acyclic graph (DAG) to parallelize service startup while honoring strict ordering requirements (e.g. ensuring network-online.target is reached before launching network daemons).

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Improperly ordered unit dependencies cause sporadic startup failures: if an application service starts before the cloud metadata server or network stack is fully initialized, API credential retrieval fails. Cloud architects author declarative systemd units with explicit retry policies (Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=5s) to ensure resilient recovery during VM reboots or transient infrastructure faults.

OS Login documents the administrative access boundary; it does not specify a universal custom application unit or promise remote dependencies are healthy when a target is reached. Architectural application: inspect the authored unit and current manager state rather than inferring readiness from VM boot. The transient user-service checkpoint tests an actual unit lifecycle, while boot ordering and cloud shutdown remain documentation-level context.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: Signals are asynchronous notifications sent by the kernel to a process to notify it of system events. Standard termination proceeds via SIGTERM (Signal 15): the process can intercept SIGTERM with a custom signal handler, allowing it to stop accepting new requests, drain active database transactions, flush write buffers, remove lockfiles, and exit cleanly. In contrast, SIGKILL (Signal 9) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored: the kernel immediately purges the process address space and reclaims resources without allowing any application cleanup.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud platforms frequently terminate processes: rolling container deployments, VM live migrations, spot instance preemptions, and autoscaling scale-downs all trigger process teardown. If microservices do not handle SIGTERM gracefully within the cloud provider's grace period (e.g. 30 seconds on GKE/Cloud Run), the platform issues SIGKILL, truncating active user requests and causing data corruption or duplicate message processing.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to GCP:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to GCP: For a Linux application on a GCP guest, a granted login permission and a delivered signal are separate controls. OS Login provides the documented host access context; Linux signal disposition determines whether the application performs graceful cleanup. Architectural application: capture the configured supervisor timeout, handler logs and final status, then check downstream completion independently. This exercise defines no GKE grace-period default or Spot VM warning guarantee, and makes no cloud termination measurement.

paragraphs.label: What it is in general:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: What it is in general: When a process terminates, it delivers an 8-bit Exit Status (0–255) to its parent via the wait() system call. By convention, exit code 0 signifies successful completion, while non-zero codes indicate errors (e.g. 1 for general error, 126 for command invoked cannot execute, 127 for command not found). When a process is killed by an unhandled signal, the shell exit code is 128 + signal_number (e.g. 143 for SIGTERM [128+15], 137 for SIGKILL [128+9]). Systemd captures stdout/stderr and termination wait statuses in the binary system journal, queried via journalctl.

paragraphs.label: Relevance to a cloud architect:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Relevance to a cloud architect: Diagnosing distributed system outages requires correlating exit codes and timestamps: an exit code of 137 in Kubernetes or Cloud Run suggests SIGKILL under the shell convention, but does not by itself distinguish an OOM kill, a shutdown deadline, an administrator kill, or an explicit application exit with that value. Architects leverage centralized structured logging to alert on non-zero exit codes and capture diagnostic traces across large VM fleets.

Configure a receiver and logging pipeline appropriate to the host; installing an agent alone does not establish that every application journal or stream is collected. Architectural application: retain local unit-scoped journal evidence and separately verify the intended Cloud Logging ingestion path and fields. This local exercise stops at the manager and journal; it does not install an agent, configure cloud ingestion or demonstrate delivery to Cloud Logging.

paragraphs.label: Concrete example:
paragraphs.paragraph_html: Concrete example: An asynchronous background worker service processes orders from a queue. When an administrator initiates a rolling deployment, systemd sends SIGTERM to the worker process (PID 4821). The worker's SIGTERM signal handler intercepts the signal, completes the in-flight order transaction, flushes log entries to stdout (fd 1), writes a durable commit record to database storage, and exits cleanly with exit code 0 within 4 seconds. The systemd journal records the timestamped shutdown sequence. Contrastingly, if an administrator executes kill -9 4821 (SIGKILL), the kernel abruptly terminates the process: the outcome of in-flight database transactions must be checked at the database, queue messages not durably acknowledged can remain eligible for replay, and the process exits with status 137, triggering message redelivery and duplicate fulfillment unless guarded by an idempotency key.

findings.rule: Factual accuracy; credentials(7) DESCRIPTION
findings.old_str: What it is in general: Every Linux process executes under a set of kernel credentials: a Real User ID (RUID), an Effective User ID (EUID) used for permission checks, a Real Group ID (RGID), an Effective Group ID (EGID), and an array of Supplementary Groups. When a process issues an open() system call, the kernel evaluates credentials in strict priority: (1) If process EUID matches file owner UID, owner bits apply; (2) Else if process EGID or any supplementary GID matches file GID, group bits apply; (3) Otherwise, other bits apply. Evaluation stops at the first matching class—if the user matches the owner class and owner bits deny read, group bits are never checked.
findings.proposed_new_str: What it is in general: Every Linux process executes under a set of kernel credentials: a Real User ID (RUID), an Effective User ID (EUID) normally tracked by its filesystem user ID (FSUID), a Real Group ID (RGID), an Effective Group ID (EGID), and an array of Supplementary Groups. When a process issues an open() system call, the kernel evaluates credentials in strict priority: (1) If process FSUID matches file owner UID, owner bits apply; (2) Else if process filesystem GID (FSGID) or any supplementary GID matches file GID, group bits apply; (3) Otherwise, other bits apply. Evaluation stops at the first matching class—if the user matches the owner class and owner bits deny read, group bits are never checked.
findings.change: Use Linux filesystem IDs for file checks while retaining the normal effective-ID relationship.

findings.rule: Unsupported tamper-evidence assurance
findings.old_str: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud architects mandate least privilege by restricting sudo permissions to specific immutable administrative binaries and prohibiting interactive root shells (sudo su -). Auditing sudo execution via systemd journals and centralized security SIEMs provides tamper-evident logs for SOC2 and ISO 27001 compliance.
findings.proposed_new_str: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud architects mandate least privilege by restricting sudo permissions to specific immutable administrative binaries and prohibiting interactive root shells (sudo su -). Architectural recommendation: audit delegated commands and protect the collection path independently. Host-local journals or a centralized destination alone do not establish tamper evidence or compliance; assess retention, access and integrity controls separately.
findings.change: Replace the blanket compliance assurance with bounded architectural guidance.

findings.rule: Orphan and zombie supervisor ownership
findings.old_str: What it is in general: A Process is an executing instance of a program, encapsulating an isolated virtual memory address space (code, data, heap, stack), a set of file descriptors, and kernel execution state. In Linux, new processes are created via the fork() (or clone()) system call, creating a child process that inherits memory pages with copy-on-write (COW) semantics. The child typically invokes execve() to replace its address space with a new executable. Each process receives a unique integer Process ID (PID) allocated by the kernel, managed under PID 1 (systemd or init), which adopts orphaned processes and reaps terminating zombie processes.
findings.proposed_new_str: What it is in general: A Process is an executing instance of a program, encapsulating an isolated virtual memory address space (code, data, heap, stack), a set of file descriptors, and kernel execution state. In Linux, new processes are created via the fork() (or clone()) system call, creating a child process that inherits memory pages with copy-on-write (COW) semantics. The child typically invokes execve() to replace its address space with a new executable. Each process receives a unique integer Process ID (PID) allocated by the kernel, within its PID namespace. A parent collects its terminated child’s wait status; an orphan can be reparented to the nearest living ancestor subreaper, or the namespace init when no such subreaper applies. PID 1 is not the direct supervisor of every process.
findings.change: Distinguish parent reaping, subreapers and namespace init.

findings.rule: RSS-only memory-limit model
findings.old_str: Relevance to a cloud architect: Understanding the process lifecycle is foundational for container and VM architecture. In container environments, PID 1 inside the container namespace must properly forward signals to child processes and reap zombie processes to prevent PID exhaustion. Furthermore, architects size memory limits based on process resident set size (RSS) rather than virtual memory size (VMS) to prevent kernel Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminations.
findings.proposed_new_str: Relevance to a cloud architect: Understanding the process lifecycle is foundational for container and VM architecture. In container environments, PID 1 inside the container namespace must properly forward signals to child processes and reap zombie processes to prevent PID exhaustion. Furthermore, resident set size (RSS) is useful process evidence, but is not the complete cgroup memory budget. Compare it with the cgroup and descendant usage reported by memory.current and the applicable memory statistics and limit; virtual address-space size alone is also insufficient. A limit can still be exhausted even when one process’s RSS appears small.
findings.change: Qualify process RSS against aggregate cgroup accounting.

findings.defect_class: Live migration and shared grace-period claims
findings.rule: Product claims require correct, product-specific supporting sections
findings.old_str: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud platforms frequently terminate processes: rolling container deployments, VM live migrations, spot instance preemptions, and autoscaling scale-downs all trigger process teardown. If microservices do not handle SIGTERM gracefully within the cloud provider's grace period (e.g. 30 seconds on GKE/Cloud Run), the platform issues SIGKILL, truncating active user requests and causing data corruption or duplicate message processing.
findings.proposed_new_str: Relevance to a cloud architect: Cloud platforms frequently terminate processes: rolling deployments, applicable preemption events and scale-downs can trigger teardown. Do not generalize one 30-second timeout to GKE and Cloud Run; their shutdown contracts differ.

findings.defect_class: Normal exit versus signal wait status
findings.rule: Normal exit versus signal wait status
findings.old_str: What it is in general: When a process terminates, it delivers an 8-bit Exit Status (0–255) to its parent via the wait() system call. By convention, exit code 0 signifies successful completion, while non-zero codes indicate errors (e.g. 1 for general error, 126 for command invoked cannot execute, 127 for command not found). When a process is killed by an unhandled signal, the shell exit code is 128 + signal_number (e.g. 143 for SIGTERM [128+15], 137 for SIGKILL [128+9]). Systemd captures stdout/stderr and termination wait statuses in the binary system journal, queried via journalctl.
findings.proposed_new_str: What it is in general: The parent obtains a wait status that distinguishes normal exit from signal termination. For a normal exit, the least significant eight bits supply the Exit Status (0–255); they are not the complete representation of every termination. By convention, exit code 0 signifies successful completion, while non-zero codes indicate errors (e.g. 1 for general error, 126 for command invoked cannot execute, 127 for command not found). When a process is killed by an unhandled signal, Bash presents a signal-derived status as 128 + signal_number (e.g. 143 for SIGTERM [128+15], 137 for SIGKILL [128+9]). Systemd captures stdout/stderr and termination wait statuses in the binary system journal, queried via journalctl.
findings.change: Separate normal exit bits, signal status and the Bash presentation.
